->Regarding this<-
# EDITION.

## Summary.

I. 1. *Reason for the new Edition of this life.* 2. *The entire Essence and reality of Christianity is vividly and solidly contained within it.* 3. *One must not dwell on a few minor, incidental difficulties.* 4. *But rather hold to the substance, which is of unquestionable and universal edification.* <note>The author encourages readers to focus on the spiritual benefits of the text rather than getting caught up in minor historical or theological quibbles.</note>

II. 5, 6, 7. *That the Life of Mr. de Renty is an effective, solid, and authorized* DEFENSE <note>original: "APOLOGIE"; in this context, it refers to a formal justification or defense of a belief system.</note> *of* MYSTICAL THEOLOGY, *and of its ways and Maxims.* 8. *Testimonies of Protestants given to this life.* <note>It was notable at the time that even those outside the Catholic Church (Protestants) respected de Renty's piety.</note>

III. *The life of Mr. de Renty, although very active, does not prejudice* <note>The sentence ends abruptly here, as is common with catchwords. The full thought likely explains that his busy life of service did not hinder his deep prayer life.</note>

### II.

5. I wish that this consideration could be of some use to us regarding an important matter which has recently been contested and debated—not without heat and passion—in several parts of Christendom, and in which all sorts of people, even the most worldly and those who are the most ignorant and incapable, have wanted to involve themselves in passing judgment. It is <term>MYSTICAL THEOLOGY: The study or experience of direct communion with God</term> and true *spirituality* of which I wish to speak, as well as its *Maxims*, its *ways of Prayer* <note>original: "voies d’Oraiſon"; refers to specific methods of meditative or contemplative prayer</note>, and its practices, which some have tried to pass off as daydreams

and extravagances; others for errors and illusions; others as a source of pride, or for impieties or things that lead to them; and others for laziness, idleness, and as the true means of becoming useless to one's neighbor and to human society. <term>Monsieur de Renty: Gaston de Renty (1611–1649), a French nobleman and philanthropist renowned for his intense devotion and service to the poor</term> was neither a dreamer nor extravagant: he was never suspected of error, nor illusion, nor pride; and even the boldest effrontery would not have dared to suggest the slightest shadow of impiety or dissolution regarding him. 6. In all conscience, is all of this not an effective Apology for <term>Mystical Theology</term><note>A branch of theology focusing on the soul's direct, subjective experience of the divine union.</note>, for its maxims and its ways—an apology worth a thousand others in formal style and on paper? Could the tree truly be bad (contrary to the assertion of *Jesus Christ*) and be judged bad, when it produces fruits as excellent as those seen in his life? Let us do so, then, for the greatest glory of God, who is admirable in his Saints; and for that of his Son Our Lord JESUS CHRIST, who overwhelmed this rare man with his graces, and communicated his Spirit to him abundantly; and let us do so aided by their help, of which I have very great need, and which I also ask of them with all my heart.

As he naturally possessed a very good mind <note>original: "eſprit"</note>, a penetrating intelligence, and great judgment, he made notable progress and appeared with brilliance in his studies; from which, nevertheless, he was withdrawn at the age of seventeen and placed in the *Academy in Paris* <note>A finishing school for young noblemen, focusing on horsemanship, fencing, and social graces alongside academics.</note>, where he became very skilled and very adept in all exercises. 5. this first time. The Bookseller having brought him another day some books which he needed, presented this one to him again, and even begged him with persistence to be willing to read it. He yielded at this stroke, and read it, and was so enlightened and so touched by it (as already before him a great multitude of all sorts of people had been), that taking up other thoughts and other affections, he resolved to apply himself seriously to his salvation, and to give himself to God: so that among the great fruits that this little Book has produced, and among the signal victories it has won, one must include this operation of grace and this change in Monsieur de Renty; who also thereafter had such esteem and such love for it, that he carried it everywhere upon his person, and helped himself with it in all his needs.

7. # Part I. Chapter I.

Vire to assist at the Estates of Normandy <note>The "Estates" were provincial assemblies that advised the King and discussed local taxation and administration.</note>, which were held at Rouen, and over which Monsieur de Longueville <note>Henri II d'Orléans, Duke of Longueville (1595–1663), a high-ranking prince and Governor of Normandy.</note> presided; where he spoke so pertinently and so prudently of affairs, that the three Estates <note>The Three Estates consisted of the Clergy, the Nobility, and the Commoners (Third Estate).</note> remained not only satisfied, but even astonished.

10. After these exercises of the nobility, he applied himself to the rebuilding of the Church of Beni as it is seen today; and far from taking the diversions customary for Lords of his rank and age, he was regularly awake every day at four o'clock; and then he would go softly, without waking his valet, into his study to pray to God; and from there at five o'clock to the Church, and to his building site; from which he did not return until about seven or eight o'clock in the evening, even having his food brought to him there, and working continually with the laborers. We cannot doubt that such an action, performed by a person of this quality and this age, and with such fervor, was very pleasing to God, and acquired for him great graces; since one heroic action prepares a soul for them more, and renders it more capable of them, than a great number of small and common ones.

->His Marriage; and how he lived until<-

<margin>1.</margin> Although the Religious state <note>The "Religious state" refers to the consecrated life of monks, nuns, or friars living under vows.</note> is—as faith teaches us and as the Church has defined—much more perfect than that of Marriage: nevertheless, the perfection of a man does not consist in the perfection of the state he has embraced; but in doing precisely the will of God, and in conducting himself in an eminent manner within the condition where God has placed him. God, in order not to deprive Monsieur de Renty entirely of the glory and merit of the Religious life, had given him the desire for it, and inspired the plan for its fulfillment, toward which he made great efforts; but having resolved to propose him to all married persons within the Church as a perfect and complete pattern of all the virtues necessary to the state of marriage, He called him to it; of which he said with great certainty, that he could not doubt it.

could, MONSIEUR DE RENTY encountered by good fortune and by a singular providence of God over him, in his lodging, a poor old woman, who had remained alone in the entire village and who had been unable to flee with the others, because she was dying as much from hunger as from illness. He consoles this poor woman, and succors her in her extremity both spiritually and corporally: for which she, feeling herself obliged to him, asked him if he was with the King’s troops, or those of the Duke of Lorraine? <note>Charles IV, Duke of Lorraine, whose lands were a major theater of conflict during the Thirty Years' War.</note> To which he, out of prudence, did not answer directly: but asked her why she inquired about that? Then she told him that if he were with the King’s troops, he should decamp soon; because the <term>Cravates</term> <note>original: "Cravates." Having received this advice, he communicated it to those who commanded with him, who all together judged it appropriate to mount their horses, to decamp <term>à la sourdine</term> <note>literally "with a mute"; to depart secretly and quietly without sounding trumpets.</note>, and to retreat to where the main body of their army was. # CHAPTER III.

*His entire change, his call to a high perfection: his outward spiritual exercises.*

1. Monsieur de Renty having lived in this manner in his marriage until the age of twenty-seven, it pleased God to touch him even more deeply, to enlighten him with more vivid lights, and to call him to that high perfection <note>a technical term in 17th-century spirituality referring to a state of complete union with God's will</note> at which—through the faithful cooperation he gave to his calling—we have seen him arrive; and, like a great torch, spread its rays in Paris and in all the places where he has been. This occurred during a mission held by the Fathers of the Oratory <note>a society of secular priests founded in France by Pierre de Bérulle</note> six or seven leagues from Paris, where he went on foot, and where he made his general Confession with all the care taken by those who wish to make it very well. He received so many graces in this new vocation that he marked this time as the beginning of his entire conversion to God, and of his perfect consecration to His service.

# CHAPTER IV.

## Of the Virtues of Monsieur de Renty in General.

<margin>I.</margin>
Before speaking of the virtues of this man-of-God <note>original: "homme-de-Dieu"</note> in detail, I believe it will be useful to say something about them in general, and to provide a sort of blueprint; regarding which I have two things to say.

The first is that among all the pious persons I have known well, I have seen none whose virtues were, in my opinion—after having well considered all things—more solid, more strong, and more complete than his. I speak in this manner for having known him intimately for several years and until his death; so much so that when I picture him in all the details of his conduct, both regarding his interior life and his exterior actions, I cannot help but form a very high idea of him, and represent him to myself as a model of consummate perfection. All those who had any connection with him (the number of whom is very great, because of the duties he performed for his neighbor) will easily agree with this, and will bear wit—

4. This is the writing that he gave to his Director <note>Director: A spiritual guide or confessor who provided personal instruction on the soul's progress</note>. Those who read it will undoubtedly judge—provided they understand it well and penetrate to the very depths of the meaning of his words—that the virtues of this excellent servant of God were very great, and his perfection very lofty. They should believe this all the more because they can be certain that he did not exaggerate in reporting things concerning himself; rather, he diminished them, being by grace, and even by nature, extremely reserved and very deliberate in all that he said, and especially concerning himself.

## I. §. SINGLE SECTION.

### *The source from which these virtues flowed.*

5. IF we now wish to examine the principle of these virtues and of this perfection, and the source from which they flowed, we will find that it was the intimate union he had with **Our Lord JESUS CHRIST**, to which he always devoted himself above all else.

6. ## PART.
### THE VIRTUES THAT perfected him with regard to himself.

## CHAPTER ONE.
### *His penances & his austerities.*

---

As our flesh and our senses are by their nature—and even more so because of their corruption <note>A reference to the theological concept of Original Sin, which was believed to have tainted human nature, making the body's desires naturally prone to straying from spiritual goals.</note>—strongly opposed to the spiritual life, and are, among the enemies of our salvation and our perfection, those which become the most troublesome and the most violent; God is accustomed to inspire those whom He wishes to raise to the height of virtue and make into saints, at the beginning of their conversion <note>In 17th-century spirituality, "conversion" often referred to a "second conversion"—a moment of profound spiritual awakening or a total commitment to the pursuit of holiness, rather than a change of religion.</note>, with a spirit of penance and mortification <term>mortification: the practice of self-denial or physical discipline (such as fasting or wearing a hairshirt) intended to subdue the physical "passions" and align the soul more closely with God.</term> of their body. 3. 8. What he did for the mortification of taste, he practiced constantly for all the other senses: for sight, for hearing, for smell, and for touch. Having gone to Pontoise on a winter day when it was very cold, he earnestly prayed the Portress <term>Tourriere: a lay sister in a convent who managed the "turn" (a rotating cabinet) to facilitate communication and deliveries between the cloistered nuns and the outside world.</term> of the Carmelite Mothers, with whom he was staying, that no fire should be made for him, and that no bed should be prepared for him; after having spoken to several Nuns, taking leave of the last one, he said to her: "we must go make our little visits." This meant visiting the prisoners and the "shamefaced poor" <term>pauvres honteux: a specific class of the poor in 17th-century France—individuals of previously higher social status who had fallen into poverty but were too embarrassed to beg publicly.</term>, and employing himself in other works of charity, which he never forgot, regardless of the weather, and no matter how little leisure time he had. He returned around nine o’clock in the evening when the Nuns were going to say Matins <term>Matines: the first and longest prayer service of the Divine Office, traditionally recited in the middle of the night or very late evening.</term>; and without wanting to take anything to eat, he entered the Church and set himself to prayer, which he continued until eleven o'clock; and then he retired to his room without allowing any fire to be made for him, even though, by his own confession, the cold bothered him greatly.

To speak truly, as we see that the more one fills oneself with one thing, the less room there is for that which is its opposite; the deeper one sinks into darkness, the less one is capable of light; and since there is nothing (as we have said above) so opposed to the spirit as the flesh; one must necessarily infer that the more a man pampers his flesh, devotes himself to his body, and takes greater care of it; the further he moves away from the spirit, and the less he prepares himself for the spiritual life.

<margin>10.</margin> This high esteem and sincere affection, which this great servant of God <note>A title commonly used for Gaston de Renty, a prominent 17th-century French nobleman who devoted his life to charity and mysticism.</note> held for the deprivation of the goods of this world, and that excellent poverty of spirit which he had achieved, could not be contained within nor remain locked inside his soul. For instance, he got rid of certain books he used simply because they were richly bound. He wore only very simple and plain clothing.

# The Life of Monsieur de Renty.

He did not use gloves, whatever the weather might be, or at least it was a very rare thing to see him wear them; indeed, his hands were so busy with acts of charity <note>Gaston de Renty was famous for personally visiting the sick and poor, often performing manual labor to assist them.</note> that he had no leisure to glove them. He kept money only to give alms and to employ it in good works; and he went on increasing in this exterior poverty and in this effective cutting back. I saw him at the beginning going by coach with a Page and Lackeys; afterward, in a coach with one Lackey, but without a Page; then, without a coach, on foot with a Lackey; and finally, alone, without a Lackey, and thus without his "self" <note>A reference to the mystical practice of self-annihilation or "dying to oneself," where one sheds all social status and ego to be empty before God.</note>.

<margin>12.</margin> Speaking one day to a very trusted person regarding Evangelical Poverty <term>Evangelical Poverty: The voluntary renunciation of worldly goods to live according to the counsels of the Gospels, following the example of Jesus.</term>, he told them that God had given him such ardent desires to possess it that, being unable—because of the ties that held him <note>As a married nobleman with children, de Renty was legally and morally obligated to maintain his family’s estate and could not simply give everything away or enter a monastery.</note>—to abandon his goods as he would have wished, in order to follow (not as a rich man, but as a poor man) JESUS CHRIST His Son, made poor for us; he tried to get by with the least he possibly could. He tried to cut back for his own person not only the superfluous and the comfortable, but even everything that was not precisely necessary. ## CHAPTER III.
### *His Humility.*

<margin>1.</margin> Poverty followed austerity and the mortification <note>In a religious context, "mortification" refers to the practice of self-denial or physical discipline to overcome sin and bring the body under the control of the soul.</note> of the body, as having a great connection with it; and humility follows poverty, especially considering that according to Saint Augustine <note>A 4th-century bishop and theologian whose writings were foundational to Western Christianity and highly influential in the 17th century.</note>, the "poverty of spirit" of which Our Lord speaks in the first Beatitude <note>Referring to the Sermon on the Mount in the Gospel of Matthew: "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."</note> is nothing other than humility. Indeed, there are no people in the world more poor in spirit than the truly humble; insofar as they consider themselves to be nothing, to have nothing, to be able to do nothing, and to be worth nothing; but rather to be the refuse and sweepings of the earth, in need of everything, and they attribute no praise to themselves for anything whatsoever. Monsieur de Renty reached this point, and he possessed this virtue to the highest degree of its excellence.

<margin>24.</margin> Driven by this spirit, he felt an ardent desire—though always maintained within his usual peace and his total abandonment <term>abandonment: in this context, a spiritual state of surrendering one’s will entirely to God’s providence.</term> to God’s orders—to receive contempt. From the abundance of his heart, he said to one person: "I would take great pleasure, if it were permitted, in going out naked in my shirt <note>In the 17th century, the "chemise" was an undergarment or tunic. <margin>25.</margin> From this, we should learn two things: First, that God sometimes gives holy souls thoughts, affections, and desires so elevated above common experience and human reason that they appear extravagant—such as the one He gave to Monsieur de Renty, and which our founder Saint Ignatius <note>Saint Ignatius of Loyola (1491–1556), founder of the Society of Jesus (Jesuits), who famously desired to be mocked for the sake of Christ.</note> had before him.

### The Life of Monsieur de Renty.

28. The humility of heart in which Monsieur de Renty was profoundly established produced in him a humility of speech, which prevented him from ever saying anything that hinted even slightly of boastfulness, or that carried the least tint of arrogance and self-esteem, or that was uttered in a haughty manner, with an imperious or self-important tone; but on the contrary, his words were all steeped in humility and modesty. As he truly considered himself a sinner, cowardly, ungrateful, treacherous, and ignorant, he likewise gave himself these names and described himself by these titles. We have already seen something of this above, to which we shall further add what he sent in a message to one person:

### II. Part. Chap. III. §. 2.

...such a grace in speaking ill of himself and in shaming himself <note>original: "se confondre" — to experience a holy sense of embarrassment or abasement in light of God's majesty</note>, that many remarked and experienced that the words of humility and abasement he spoke about himself impressed his very disposition onto those who heard him speak, and brought into their souls a sense of smallness, and gave them feelings of humility.

32. ### 3. §. SECTION THREE.

#### *His Humility in actions.*

34. After humility of heart and of words comes that of actions, which Monsieur de Renty practiced excellently. We have already seen this in several encounters; we shall see it yet again in many others, and particularly when we speak of his patience and his charity toward the poor and the sick; but beyond that, we say that he was continually attentive to all opportunities for humility, and that he did not let a single one escape without making use of it.

### 4. §. SECTION FOUR.

#### *His Love for the Hidden Life.*

47. **W**e also count as an effect of his humility the love he had for the hidden and unknown life; <note>The "hidden life" refers to a spiritual practice, modeled on the thirty years Jesus spent in Nazareth before his public ministry, focusing on interior prayer and avoiding public recognition.</note> for he loved it not only to be able to devote himself more fully to God and to commune more at leisure with Our Lord, who was the dear object of his heart: but furthermore to have the means to flee the esteem, honor, and praise of men, and to be erased from their minds and forgotten by the whole world.

48. Pressed by this love, he would say that if God had not bound him to the state <note>In this context, "state" refers to his "state of life" or vocation as a married nobleman and father, which carried social and religious obligations he could not abandon.</note> in which he was, he would have gone to some foreign and distant land to live there hidden for the rest of his days; that he wished to be known by no one on earth; that it was not even expedient for anyone to even know he existed; and that it would have been a special pleasure for him to be banished from the hearts of all men, and ignored by all creatures <note>original: "creatures"; in 17th-century theology, this refers to any created being—human, animal, or angel—as distinct from the Creator.</note>: To which end he contributed everything he could on his part, doing nothing that might have brought him recognition or gained him affection; and it was noted,

# CHAPTER IV.

->*The contempt he held for the world.*<-

I. This great affection that Monsieur de Renty held for the <term>hidden life</term> <note>A spiritual practice, popular in 17th-century French mysticism, of withdrawing the soul from social vanity and public recognition to live in constant, private communion with God.</note> was an evident sign of the contempt he held for the world; for had he esteemed it, he would not have wished to leave it. To express now the degree to which he despised it would be very difficult. It is enough for us to know that he held it in extreme contempt to observe, from what we have reported above, how he renounced—as much as was in his power—all that the world can promise and give, and with which it enslaves and captivates men; how he <term>degraded himself</term> <note>In this context, "degrading" oneself refers to a voluntary lowering of social rank or the refusal to act according to the prideful expectations of the nobility.</note> from his own nobility; how he made a <term>cession of his goods</term> <note>A legal surrender of his property and assets. Renty sought to divest himself of legal ownership so he could live as a "steward" for the poor rather than a wealthy master.</note> and stripped himself of their ownership, so as to use them only in the capacity of a poor man; how he weaned himself from pleasures, and rejected the honors and dignities to which his birth and his excellent perfections gave him [entitlement]...

13. **T**HIS great patience that Monsieur de Renty <note>Gaston de Renty (1611–1649) was a French nobleman and mystic known for his intense devotion and charitable works.</note> possessed flowed from the high esteem in which he held sufferings, knowing that when they are well received, they are sources of eternal life, mines of gold and celestial riches, and participations in the cross of Our Lord, which God has made the cause of our salvation and of all the goods we shall ever possess; to which, consequently, all those who wish to be saved must be linked.

26. After having thus prepared himself for some time, he went to find his Lady Mother, and cast himself on his knees before her in an act of reverence, humility, and submission capable of softening the most hardened hearts. This he did not do just once, but several times, and with a great abundance of tears; and he entreated her, using the most persuasive words he could find, that she would be pleased to house him and his whole family with her, and maintain him as she saw fit, and that afterwards she might dispose of all the wealth his Father had left him.

## CHAPTER VI.

### *His Mortification.* <note>In the 17th century, "mortification" referred to the spiritual practice of "dying to oneself"—disciplining the body and the ego to better align one's soul with God.</note>

1. WHAT we have said thus far in this second part regarding the austerities, poverty, humility, and patience of **Monsieur de Renty** <note>Gaston de Renty (1611–1649) was a French nobleman and famous mystic known for his intense devotion and service to the poor.</note>, clearly shows to what extent he was mortified, and that he was a true grain of that mysterious wheat of which Our Lord speaks, which dies, and by its death bears much fruit. But beyond this, we will touch upon some other effects of his mortification here.

<margin>(a) Luke 9: 23.</margin>
The entire secret of the Christian life consists in destroying that which is corrupt in our nature, in order to make room within ourselves for grace, and to make the **old man** <note>A biblical term (from the writings of St. Paul) referring to a person's unregenerate, sinful nature before spiritual rebirth.</note> die so that **JESUS CHRIST** may live there; He taught us that this is only achieved through continual mortification, and for this purpose told us: (a) *If anyone does not carry his cross, and do so every day, he cannot be my Disciple.*

2. This excellent Disciple of this great Master, having well understood his doctrine,

->Part II. Chapter VI.<-

from the very beginning of his conversion, [he] applied all his care to mortify himself in everything, to tame his passions, to regulate his internal and external movements, to annihilate his desires and die to all the inclinations of his **spoiled nature** <note>original: *nature gâtée*; a 17th-century theological term referring to human nature corrupted by original sin, which was believed to be inherently prone to selfishness.</note>, with such faithfulness and constancy that as soon as he perceived that his nature was leaning toward something with imperfection, and that his natural will inclined in one direction, he would do the exact opposite. He told a very close confidant that he had taken it upon himself to resist his nature in everything, and that with the grace of God, he had always overcome himself. Thus, he proceeded in all things with a spirit of death and continual sacrifice, no longer making any use of his passions, his senses, or anything within him, except with an eye always open to prevent the operation of **malignant nature** <note>original: *nature maligne*; refers to the human ego’s tendency to act out of self-interest rather than divine will.</note> and what it might try to insert of its own. Following the guidance of **Our Lord**, he said that one must detach oneself from oneself and from every created object, so that God alone might be our object.

10. He told another person that the love a Christian soul was obliged to have for the virtues that **JESUS CHRIST** taught us should not end in simple feelings of esteem and respect. ### CHAPTER ONE.

*His application to Our Lord* JESUS CHRIST *with regard to his Neighbor.*

<image-desc>A decorative drop cap letter 'N' with an engraved design of scrolling foliage and flowers.</image-desc>

**W**e have remarked in the first Part of this History, that the great exercise of Monsieur de Renty <note>Gaston de Renty (1611–1649) was a French aristocrat and a prominent figure in the 17th-century Catholic "French School" of spirituality, known for his dedication to the poor.</note> was to apply and unite himself to Our Lord JESUS CHRIST; and from the union he had with him, and from his examples, to let all his virtues and all his good works flow forth. This was the general method he maintained in everything. He modeled himself upon him to compose his interior and his exterior <term>Interior and exterior: These terms refer to the "inner life" of the soul (thoughts and prayers) and the "outer life" (actions and physical bearing).</term>, and never lifted his eyes from this divine Original, striving to trace his features exactly upon himself, to take on his true lineaments <term>Lineaments: Distinctive features or characteristic outlines; here, De Renty is portrayed as an artist attempting to paint Christ’s character onto his own soul.</term>, and to make himself into his natural and perfect copy.

2. This was the goal of all his designs and all his cares, and particularly regarding charity toward his neighbor <note>Original: "charité du prochain." In 17th-century spirituality, this refers to the active love and service of others as a reflection of one's love for God.</note>, for which he took Our Lord as his great Exemplar; this is why he looked upon what He did and what He endured for men; he considered the affections and the tenderness He had for them; how He sought them out, how He conversed with them, how He instructed them, how He consoled and encouraged them, how He rebuked them, how He bore with them in their faults, and how He held them all dearly embraced in His spirit and pressed lovingly to His heart.

3. 11. One must act in this way to do good and to avoid receiving harm. He who does not do so puts himself in danger of both receiving much harm and doing very little good. If one proceeds by natural impulse and motive <note>In 17th-century spirituality, "nature" refers to human instincts and desires unguided by divine grace, which were seen as inherently flawed.</note>, the effects will reflect their cause, and will be nothing but natural or vicious; or at most, indifferent: losses of time, light discourse, amusement, mental attachments, and affections that are rooted in the senses, only to degenerate later into something worse; so that while wanting to purify a person, one soils oneself; and thinking to save them, one often damns oneself. He who wishes to lead souls to **Jesus Christ** and to God must necessarily lead them by the paths that lead there.

### I. §. FIRST SECTION.

#### *His Charity toward the Poor.*

<margin>14.</margin> FIRSTLY, I have to say regarding the affection that Monsieur de Renty <note>Gaston de Renty was a prominent figure in the French School of Spirituality, known for his "interior life" and practical philanthropy.</note> bore toward the poor, and the charity he exercised toward them, that Jesus Christ was not only the source for giving him the grace for it; but also the motive and the object; because he looked upon Him in them, and it was Him whom he thought to assist and serve in their persons; so that he did not stop at their torn and patched clothes, nor at all their vile and contemptible exterior, which naturally displeases the eyes, and offends the sense of smell and the other senses: but passing further, he saw therein, and beneath that, with the eyes of faith, Our Lord Jesus Christ, present and resident in them, and considered them as His living images <note>original: "naïves images," here meaning natural, authentic, or true-to-life representations.</note>, whom He loves and whom He esteems. Beyond this charity, and many others—whether in alms or other forms of assistance of all kinds that Monsieur de Renty performed within his own home—he worked for the relief of all the poor of Paris, and even those much further away, in every way possible for him. He occupied himself with learning their needs; he thought of the means to provide a remedy, and subsequently applied his care to them; and, being unable to do everything himself, he employed other people to help; he spoke for them; he petitioned for them; he himself bought the items they needed and then carried these to them. He sought out establishments and positions <note>original: *conditions*; this refers to finding stable employment or domestic service placements for those in need.</note> for men, children, and young women who lacked them; and being sometimes unable to find such a place immediately, he kept and fed some of them in his own house for a long time, until he had settled them well.

20. Regarding their temporal <note>In this context, "temporal" refers to worldly or physical needs, such as food and money, as opposed to "spiritual" needs like prayer or confession.</note> necessities, he would consider the ability, industriousness, trade, and employment of each person. If they were artisans <term>artisans: skilled manual workers or craftsmen who owned their own tools.</term>, he observed what they lacked for their labor and to earn a living—whether it was tools, raw materials, fabrics, or a task to perform. He provided for these needs by giving them the means to acquire new tools or by redeeming those they had pawned <note>original: *dégageoit les leurs*; implying he paid the debts to recover their tools from a pawn shop so they could return to work.</note>. He supplied them with materials or bought them fabrics in kind, giving them bread for two or three days in the meantime. He found work for them, and not just for the men, but also for their wives and children, so that the whole family could sustain themselves. Afterward, he would purchase the goods they produced, which he then used for other charitable acts. He helped them find buyers for their products and encouraged them to work and avoid idleness, returning periodically to visit them and ensure all was well in their household.

21. Let us add to this his charity toward the poor prisoners, whom he visited, whom he comforted, and to whom he gave alms <note>original: *aumônes*; charitable gifts of money or food given to the poor.</note>; he procured and mediated their liberty, though always with discernment as to whether it was expedient for their salvation. For he said one day, when he was being asked to help deliver the man we are about to speak of, that people were often released from prison who afterward used their liberty only to offend God and damn themselves; and that for their own good, it was better to leave them there. Aside from such cases, he devoted himself to them with great affection, of which here is a notable example.

There was in lower Normandy a man who had been a prisoner for several years; he was innocent, yet reduced to great necessity. Many people had worked for his release, but to no effect, because he was facing a powerful opponent <note>original: *forte partie*; referring to an adversary with significant legal or social influence.</note>. Word of this was brought to Monsieur de Renty, who, being well-informed of the facts, undertook to assist this poor prisoner. He arranged to have a Master of Requests <term>Master of Requests: a high-ranking magistrate in the French judicial system who handled petitions to the King’s Council.</term>, a very virtuous man, appointed as the Rapporteur <term>Rapporteur: an official appointed by a court to examine a case and report the findings to the judges.</term> for the Council where the lawsuit was pending. He recommended the matter to his lawyer; he went to see him and petitioned him several times, and he promised to cover all the necessary expenses.

### The Life of Monsieur de Renty.

But as these legal proceedings dragged on, and the prisoner remained steeped in his misery, Monsieur de Renty changed his course of action. He wrote to the opposing party <note>original: *sa partie*; the adversary or plaintiff in the legal case.</note> on the prisoner’s behalf, begging him to leave the matter in his hands; he explained that he would soon be traveling to Normandy, and that there he would find a means to settle the affair to the party's satisfaction. He set out for that province; and upon his arrival, he arranged for a Mission <term>Mission: a period of intensive preaching and charitable work, often led by the Lazarist fathers, intended to revive religious life in a specific parish.</term> to begin in his **Parish of Beni** <note>The Parish of Beni refers to Bény-Bocage in Lower Normandy, where the Renty family held estates.</note>; and a few days later, taking one of the Missionary Fathers with him, he traveled to the Town where the prisoner and his adversary were located.

When the news spread through the Town that **Monsieur de Renty** was arriving, all the streets filled with people who blessed God for his coming; and as he knew the reason for their excitement, he remarked that only he could see this business through and put an end to the poor man’s suffering; and everyone praised God for choosing such a holy man for the task, and offered a thousand prayers for him. He then went to the prison, where the Father delivered an exhortation <note>original: *exhortation*; a formal speech or sermon intended to encourage or advise.</note> to the prisoners to comfort and strengthen them. **Monsieur de Renty** relieved their needs with his alms <note>original: *aumônes*; charitable gifts of money or food.</note>, and afterward spoke to his prisoner, telling him that he would go to see his adversary to in-

### SECTION TWO.

->*His Charity toward the Sick Poor.*<-

<margin>22.</margin> If Monsieur de Renty possessed great charity for the poor, he possessed even more for the poor who were sick, because he saw in them two distinct objects for this excellent virtue: poverty and illness. Thus, his charity was increased by half, and its fire redoubled its flame within his merciful heart toward them.

One reads of almost nothing in the lives of the greatest Saints regarding this subject that he did not also practice. His charity was so extensive, and the care he took of them went so far, that—not contenting himself with assisting the sick poor in only one or two ways—they found in him, and often during a single visit, a Benefactor, a Physician, and an Apo... <note>The word continues on the next page as *Apoticaire* (Apothecary).</note>

23. From the year 1641, he learned to bleed patients <note>original: *saigner*; bloodletting was a standard medical treatment in the 17th century</note> and perform other surgical operations. He wished to know how to prepare medications and all sorts of remedies; and by consulting with a Physician, he had himself instructed in the principal matters of Medicine. And as his goal was not mere knowledge, but practice, he always carried on his person—whether he went through the city or the countryside—medicinal powders for common ailments, and a case containing his <term>surgical instruments</term> <note>These would have included lancets for bloodletting and scalpels for basic procedures.</note> for bleeding and making incisions. He performed these with a skill and confidence that were admirable, without, however, venturing beyond his knowledge, as he was very prudent.

To this, I add the ardent desire he had that a hospital be established for those suffering from scrofula <term>écrouëlez: individuals afflicted with scrofula, a form of tuberculosis affecting the lymph nodes of the neck. It was in this manner that this great servant of God dedicated himself to the care of the sick, and specifically those whose illnesses were most repulsive. Let us see now what success and what blessing God granted to his labors.

## His zeal for the salvation of his Neighbor.

32. This Charity was even much greater and much more ardent in the late <note>The French word "feu" indicates the subject is deceased; de Renty died in 1649.</note> Monsieur de Renty than those of which we have spoken; because also, as St. Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential medieval philosopher and theologian whose works defined much of Catholic doctrine.</note> says, it is much more elevated and much more noble, first by reason of the subject, which is the soul, which this charity regards, and which is incomparably more excellent than the body, to whose care alone those others apply themselves. 33. Now, this zeal was admirable, and it possessed all the qualities necessary to be most perfect. He drew up several regulations for Gentlemen and persons of quality <term>persons of quality: (French: *personnes de qualité*) a term used in the 17th century to refer to the nobility and upper classes</term>, as well as for Ladies and young noblewomen, knowing that as these people are raised above others, they are also seen from further away; and that their example makes a greater impression for good or for evil than that of common people. I have these memoirs written in his own hand and composed in his own style, which deserve to be recorded here to demonstrate his zeal and to serve as a useful guide. They are as follows:

### 6. §. SIXTH SECTION.

#### *Continuation of the same subject.*

<margin>52.</margin>The zeal of Monsieur de Renty <note>Gaston de Renty (1611–1649) was a French nobleman who famously renounced a military career to dedicate his life and fortune to the service of the poor and the sick.</note> carried him toward all sorts of people. He had a particular inclination for supporting poor girls who were on the verge of falling into evil <note>In the social context of the time, this often referred to the danger of being driven into prostitution by poverty.</note>, or for lifting them up if they had already fallen. It would be impossible to recount all the actions of this nature that he performed, and the number of these girls whom he placed through his care—and even by contributing from his own wealth—some with the *Penitent Girls* <note>The "Filles Pénitentes" was a religious congregation established to provide a refuge and a path to reform for women who had lived on the streets.</note>, others at *The Madelaine* <note>Referring to the Convent of the Madelonnettes or the Order of Saint Mary Magdalen, institutions dedicated to the "reclamation" of fallen women.</note>, and others in the homes of virtuous ladies who employed themselves in this kind of charity. This work is all the more great and important because it does not only save a poor girl who is in danger of making a shipwreck of her honor and her salvation, or who has indeed already done so and is losing her soul; but it also prevents the **damnation** <note>The theological state of being condemned to eternal punishment.</note> of many men, and a great number of sins and a thousand disorders.

#### III. Part. Chap. II. §. 6.

53. I mentioned in the second section what his zeal led him to do at the great Hôtel-Dieu <note>The "Hôtel-Dieu" (God's House) was the traditional name for the principal hospital in French cities, which served the poor and the sick.</note> for the instruction of the poor; here is the work he undertook at the Hospital of Saint Gervais. As he was passing one day in the year 1641 in front of this hospital, he asked what purpose it served, and what works of charity were practiced there; he was told that they took in and lodged poor travelers <note>The term "passans" refers to transient people—pilgrims, itinerant laborers, or the homeless moving between towns—who were provided with temporary overnight shelter.</note>. Considering this institution, he approved of it greatly: but seeing that the poor who gathered there every evening in great numbers lacked instruction, he felt moved by God to provide it to them; and for this reason, a few days later, he came to ask with great humility and much submission for the permission of the Mother Superior of the place to come and teach them the Catechism <note>The Catechism is a summary of the principles of Christian religion used for teaching the faith.</note> in the evening, when they were all assembled: which she granted him very willingly without knowing who he was, because he had not given his name, and indeed he concealed it for the space of six months.

With this authority, he undertook this duty, which he held very dear, because every evening there are new travelers; and he came to catechize and instruct these poor people, and he came there often all alone, and on foot, in Summer and in Winter,

### 7. §. SEVENTH SECTION.

->Some other qualities of his zeal.<-

59. Since there are many things to do and many to suffer in the mission of seeking the salvation of one's neighbor, it is necessary that the zeal of the person who devotes himself to it be both courageous and patient. That of **Monsieur de Renty** possessed these two qualities to an eminent degree: for first, he was full of courage, resolute, and industrious, conducting affairs as if he had three bodies <note>A hyperbolic expression meaning he possessed the productivity and energy of three people.</note>, and accomplishing more in a half-hour than others would have done in several days; because he was strong enough to take on all necessary fatigues; and furthermore, he was expeditious and decisive.

Having found a man who had been suborned <note>In this context, the man had been bribed or manipulated, likely by those seeking to persuade him to leave the Catholic Church during the religious tensions of 17th-century France.</note> and won over to leave the Church, and who was so determined in this path that he even wanted to drag his wife along with him by force, despite whatever resistance she might offer; he spoke to him to disabuse him and to prevent the violence he was using against his wife. Afterward, he went to find the one who had seduced the man and threatened him with Justice <note>Referring to legal or judicial action through the courts.</note> if he continued his schemes regarding several others whom he had tried to pervert. Thus, with his courageous zeal, he broke all his evil designs and secured this family that was on the verge of ruin.

He added that, for this reason, the person would be doing him a great charity by being so honest with him. The other person, feeling their heart open through these words, begged him to say if he saw anything in him that he ought to know; which he then did.

# The Life of Monsieur de Renty.

[he] was by grace and even by nature very prudent and very wise; his zeal possessed all these perfections and conducted itself in everything with this enlightenment. Someone had written to him to urge him to obtain letters of abolition <term>pardon: official royal letters that completely remitted a crime and its penalty</term> for a homicide committed by a young man, on the basis that his mother promised, in exchange for this favor, eight thousand livres <note>An immense sum in the 17th century, often used as a "charitable" offering to secure legal leniency.</note> to be used for works of piety and alms. In the first response he gave, he asked if the criminal was truly repentant for his fault; but here is what he wrote back in the second:

> "I did not think I should consider obtaining these letters, because it would appear that, under the cover of money, one was seeking impunity, and one would stain <note>original: "fouilleroit," likely a variant of "souilleroit," meaning to soil or defile.</note> one's hands with the price of spilled blood. In short, even if others might undertake this without hesitation, and even though I see the considerable alms that would come from it, I nonetheless cannot apply myself to it. Divine Providence will never forget its holy Poor."

72. One of the great marks of prudence in a man of zeal is not to break down his body with excessive labors, nor to overburden his mind with affairs which, by their multitude or their weight, stifle devotion; and in taking care of the salvation of others, not to neglect—

## SECTION ELEVEN.

->*His great knowledge of interior matters.*<-

<margin>91.</margin> It must be admitted that the knowledge of interior matters is very difficult, and that the science of the spirit is, without contradiction, the most obscure of all sciences; and that unless one possesses great graces from God and is well-enlightened by the Sun of Justice <note>The "Sun of Justice" (original: *Soleil de Justice*) is a traditional Christian title for Christ, derived from the book of Malachi, representing the source of divine truth and spiritual light.</note>, it is impossible to understand much of it or to become skilled in it. If the science of treating and healing bodies is difficult and merely conjectural—because it is guided in its cures only by external signs, which are still often ambiguous and equivocal, causing even the most learned physicians to sometimes be mistaken and prescribe entirely opposite remedies—how much more so will this be true for the science of governing spirits in matters of salvation? These matters are spiritual, removed from our senses, and furthermore supernatural, and consequently filled for us with great difficul-

-ties, and shrouded in deep darkness?

Monsieur de Renty was, however, very discerning in this regard; and he had received from God admirable enlightenment to understand all its secrets and know its most hidden ways: to which his own experience also served him greatly. His greatest insights went toward discerning the true from the false, the safe from the perilous, and the movements of the good Spirit <note>In the tradition of spiritual discernment, "movements of the spirit" refers to the internal impulses, thoughts, or feelings that lead a person either toward or away from God.</note> from those of the bad: to calming souls, to strengthening them always and giving them courage, to detaching them from everything to unite them to Our Lord Jesus Christ, and through him to the Divinity, and making them act in all things by His Spirit and after His model.

<margin>92.</margin> Here are some of his insights and some rays of his light on these matters, which I find in papers written by his hand, and which will give us great clarity to see many mysteries of the spiritual life.

> (1.) There are three kinds of lifting up <note>The original term "élévation" refers to a specific form of prayer where the heart is raised toward God in a brief, intense moment of focus.</note> and groanings <note>original: "gemiffemens". In 17th-century spirituality, these are not necessarily cries of pain, but rather "sighs of the heart" or deep, wordless longings of the soul for God.</note> of the soul to God, in which it must continually be in order to be able to accomplish what Our Lord enjoins us, namely, *(a)* to pray always and never give up <note>original: "ne se relâcher jamais". This is a translation of the Latin phrase from Luke 18:1, *non deficere*, meaning to not grow weary or lose heart.</note>.

(a) Luke 18:1.

III. Part. Chap. IV.

# CHAPTER IV.

## *His Conduct in Business Affairs.*

1. IT must first be said on this subject that Monsieur de Renty was, without question, one of the busiest men in Paris and the Kingdom regarding those things that concern the service of God, and that he handled business <term>business: (French: *affaires*) In this context, the term refers not to commercial trade, but to the administration of charitable organizations, religious projects, and social welfare.</term> of this nature in countless numbers. God had granted him for this purpose a great strength of body and mind, as well as a high capacity to fulfill these duties; so that without rushing, without straining, with a composed mind and an application that was always calm, without losing a moment of time, he would do one thing, and then another, and sometimes several together. He was seen doing three things at once without being troubled or making mistakes; he was seen, when pressed by several matters that arose all at once and required immediate attention, reading letters, granting audiences <note>To "grant audience" was to receive visitors officially to hear their requests or reports, a practice common among the nobility who managed public or religious interests.</note>, and responding to different people at the same time and on various subjects, clearly and distinctly.

2. But here is the order he maintained in business affairs. He weighed and considered a matter deeply before resolving it, yet without clinging so stubbornly to his own opinion that he would not easily yield when he saw that another’s reasons were better than his own. This is necessary for all who deliberate on business, but quite rare; because everyone—if they are not careful—is an idolater of their own mind and in love with their own insights, being pleased to win out and to have their opinions prevail. Having drawn up certain regulations for a pious association <term>pious association: (French: *compagnie de piété*) A group of laypeople or clergy dedicated to charitable works and spiritual growth, common in 17th-century France.</term> which he had prepared with care, and having requested several virtuous persons to examine them, he bore their corrections with great humility and personally made the deletions, asking that other, more fitting words be used instead of his own.

3. Once a matter was decided, he showed himself prompt, firm, and steadfast in its execution, and he did not leave it until he had brought it to the necessary point. There are many who begin many affairs, but they never finish them; they have plenty of passion and strength at the start, but this passion cools during the pursuit, and this strength falters. Nature—that wise and perfect artisan—does not stop in the middle of her task when producing her works; she brings them to their fulfillment and perfection. A child does not leave its mother’s womb until it is entirely formed <note>The original French "organisé" here refers to the biological formation of the body's organs and systems.</note> and has all its limbs. Monsieur de Renty planned a matter prudently; he pursued it vigorously; and he never abandoned it, as far as it depended on him, until he had brought it to completion <note>Original: "mise à chef," an archaic expression meaning to finish or bring to a head.</note>.

4. Yet it sometimes happened, by a different way of conducting himself, that upon seeing a matter well-established and well-connected, or already on the right track and in its flow, he would leave it to one of his friends capable of finishing it; not out of inconstancy of mind, but in order to begin another, and thus to accomplish more. 13. This is the testimony provided by the memoirs sent from various locations. They state that he did not act to undertake any project, nor to bring it to completion <note>original: "mettre à chef" — an archaic French idiom meaning to finish or achieve a goal.</note>, through his own spirit or the movement of his own will. Instead, he acted by the Spirit of God, as he came to know His will. Consequently, if after beginning a task he felt this inner movement cease, he would also stop without pursuing it further. He never made any personal plans, even though he saw things that needed to be done; rather, he waited for express orders from God, which were revealed to him either by "light" in his understanding <note>term: <term>understanding</term> (French: *entendement*). Monsieur de Renty felt moved to go to Beaune, which is only seven leagues <note>A league was a measurement of distance, roughly 4 kilometers or 2.5 miles; seven leagues would be approximately 28 kilometers.</note> distant from Dijon, to commend himself to the prayers of this holy Girl <note>original: "Fille"; here referring to a "daughter" of the religious order or a nun.</note>. 18. Innocence and simplicity are two powerful aids given to purity to enable it to act without hindrance. Innocence shields it against all things that present themselves, serving as a rampart and as a very clear crystal through which the soul looks innocently upon all things: vices, wickednesses, impurities, pomps, vanities, beauties, and all other external objects.

Just as a child sees all the things offered to his eyes with a pure and innocent eye, with an unburdened view and a superficial glance—one that does not enter into the malice of things and retains no trace of them after he has seen them—a Child of grace <term>Child of grace (Enfant de grace): A person who has attained a state of spiritual "infancy," characterized by total dependence on God and a lack of worldly guile.</term> looks and acts in the same way. He applies himself to all things innocently, without receiving their malignant impressions. This is a very great and necessary aid for him in his conversation with men: to see, examine, and treat their ills without taking any of it upon himself, and to touch filth as cleanly as the rays of the Sun touch a dung-heap. <note>original: "fumier." ### CHAPTER III.

->His Hope.<-

1. A great faith produces, by a certain moral necessity <note>In 17th-century spiritual writing, "moral necessity" suggests that while a person remains free, a soul truly filled with faith cannot help but feel hope and love; it is the natural consequence of a deep conviction.</note>, a great hope and a great charity. One only needs to truly believe what God is in Himself and to us, in order to trust perfectly in Him, and to love Him ardently. As Monsieur de Renty was established in a very firm faith in God, as we have just said, he also had an unshakable confidence in Him, and a burning love for Him.

2. His confidence was grounded upon the knowledge he had of the power, the goodness, the mercy, and the generosity of God, and of the infinite merits of Our Lord <note>The "merits of Our Lord" refers to the theological belief that Jesus’s life and suffering created a "treasury" of grace that believers can rely upon for their salvation.</note>. Strengthening himself upon these foundations, he hoped for everything, and thought himself capable of everything. Considering himself, he said that he could do nothing, however small it might be; casting his sight upon God, he asserted that nothing was impossible to Him; and thus the distrust he had of himself and his humility was neither cowardly nor dejected, but courageous and magnanimous, just as it

11. As this excellent virtue infallibly gives the soul that possesses it in perfection a profound rest, a solid joy, great courage, a high elevation above all earthly things, and a generous contempt for everything the world prizes and desires, along with a delicious foretaste of the pleasures of eternal bliss—just as it is very easy for one who hopes soon to enjoy a rich Kingdom to despise a bundle of straw—it abundantly communicated all these treasures to this excellent man, and imprinted all these noble sentiments upon him. These led him to encourage souls with all his might toward this virtue, knowing by his own experience the inestimable blessings it produces; that it was our lenitive <term>lenitive: a soothing medicine or treatment that eases pain and lessens distress.</term> in all our ills, our staff and our support in our weaknesses, and our sure harbor in our storms. And he wisely warned that God, in order to make us acquire it and to give us strength in it, placed us in temptations and trials; so as to oblige us to have recourse to Him, to ask for His help, and to wait for Him in trust.

12. He gave this instruction on this subject to a person on the occasion of the terror the Apostles felt upon seeing Our Lord walking on the water and taking Him for a phantom <note>Original: "fantoſme." In the 17th century, this referred to a ghost or an apparition that causes irrational fear.</note>.

> Do you think it was without a particular providence <term>providence: God’s divine guidance and care for the world and its inhabitants.</term> that Our Lord let His Apostles go alone in a small boat and permitted a contrary wind to rise? Who does not know that it is in this way that He forms the souls of the Faithful—through His absences and through trials? And that afterward, by showing His power over the sea and over the storms, He gives life to our faith, making Himself known as the Messiah and the true Liberator of the World?
> 
> But notice that there are many people who, in their distress, share much of the terror the Apostles felt when they saw Our Lord walking on the water: everything frightens them—the wind, the waves, **JESUS CHRIST** Himself. By this, I mean the agitations of their minds, their self-conscious reflections <note>Original: "retours." This refers to the habit of "turning back" onto oneself in anxious over-analysis rather than looking toward God.</note>, and even the advice given to them to draw them out of these states and to strengthen them in **JESUS CHRIST** before God. All of this appears to them as a phantom that terrifies them, unless **JESUS** **CHRIST** reveals Himself more fully to them and strengthens them.

-> *His Love for God.* <-

<margin>I.</margin>
As the Love of God is undeniably the most excellent and the most perfect of all virtues, and the one which principally and above all others makes Saints, we cannot doubt that this holy man possessed it in an eminent degree, and that he loved God with all his heart. ## CHAPTER VI.

->*His respect for holy things.*<-

1. Mr. de Renty did not only show respect toward God; but also, as a morally necessary consequence, toward everything that concerned His service, and toward all holy and divine things. This is the sentiment that the virtue of Religion <term>Religion: In this historical context, "Religion" refers to the specific moral virtue that leads a person to render to God the honor and worship that is His due</term> impresses upon a soul, and the effect it causes that soul to produce in its outward behavior.

2. Thus, this excellent servant of God rendered a singular reverence, first of all, to holy places. It would be difficult to describe with what respect and devotion he conducted himself in Churches; when he entered them, it was to compose himself with a higher modesty and a more religious bearing. He never sat there nor covered his head <note>It was common 17th-century etiquette for men to wear hats indoors, but Renty’s refusal to do so in church—even during long sermons—was a sign of profound humility before the Divine presence</note>, even during the sermon. He remained there as long as he possibly could; and he was seen there during the Great Feasts for seven or eight hours straight on his knees. He kept a very strict silence there; and if someone, regardless of their social standing, spoke to him, he would cut the conversation short; for if the matter required

->His Devotion toward the Holy Eucharist.<-

<margin>1.</margin>One of the greatest devotions of this holy man was toward the Holy Eucharist <term>The Eucharist (or Holy Communion) is the central Christian sacrament involving the consecrated bread and wine, which Catholics believe becomes the body and blood of Christ.</term>, considered both as a Sacrifice and as a Sacrament. He held it in incredible regard, honoring it with all the respect possible to him, and he felt a very tender love for it. He praised and blessed God for its institution <note>The "institution" refers to the moment Jesus established the Eucharist during the Last Supper.</note>, and encouraged everyone, both by word of mouth and through his letters, to do the same. 

He said that it had been instituted to keep Our Lord—both God and Man—here among us, to obtain for us all the blessings of grace of which we are capable on earth, and to prepare us for the blessings of glory in heaven. He maintained that the great design of God in the Incarnation <term>The "Incarnation" refers to the theological belief that God took on human form in Jesus Christ.</term>, and in the life, death, and resurrection of his Son, had been to give us His Spirit to be our eternal life. This Spirit was taught to us by His word, earned for us by His death, and is given to us from His state of glory; and in order to give it to us, and to make us live by it while dying to ourselves <note>To "die to oneself" is a spiritual concept of setting aside one's own ego and worldly desires to be filled with the divine.</note>, He gives Himself to us in

## Part II. Chapter VII.

6. This same affection inspired him, starting in the year 1641, to form in his parish of St. Paul <note>St. Paul-des-Champs was the local parish church for the nobility living in the Marais district of Paris.</note> a company of ladies to pray every afternoon, each at her designated hour, before the Holy Sacrament. He wrote a short treatise on the conduct of this devotion and the motives for which it should be undertaken. The principal motive is to consider how Our Lord, being continually present in this adorable mystery to communicate Himself to us, it seemed very reasonable that there should also be some persons incessantly in the churches where He is, to pay Him our respects and homage, and to satisfy the desire He has to give Himself to us. In this Chapter, we shall speak of the **Prayer** <note>original: *Oraison*. In 17th-century spirituality, this specifically refers to "mental prayer" or internal meditation as opposed to simply reciting vocal prayers.</note> of this man of God; and we say that as Prayer is the great channel through which God’s gifts flow into our souls, the most certain means to acquire the help and graces necessary for our salvation, and the most general instrument we use in the spiritual life to perform all its functions, and to advance us in the **purgative** <term>purgative life: the first stage of the spiritual path, focused on cleansing the soul of sin, vices, and worldly attachments</term> for the destruction of vices and sins; in the **illuminative** <term>illuminative life: the second stage, where the believer focuses on practicing virtues and imitating Christ, receiving greater spiritual insight</term> for the practice of virtues; and in the **unitive** <term>unitive life: the final stage of spiritual perfection, characterized by a constant, intimate union of the soul with God</term> to arrive at union with God, in which our perfection consists; all the Saints have had such high esteem and such love for this divine action, that setting aside almost all others, they have spent days and nights in prayer. And many have abandoned their scepters and their crowns, and have retired to Monasteries and into solitudes, to have the honor of being able to converse and speak with God more secretly, more privately, and for a longer time.

#### Part IV, Chapter VIII, Section 1. 413
S 3

But to understand it, it is necessary to know that the Saints, speaking of Contemplation—which is the most sublime <term>Prayer: *Oraison*, a term referring specifically to interior or mental prayer rather than recited vocal prayers</term> that one can practice on earth—teach us that there are two kinds: one is *Acquired*, and the other is *Infused*.

The *Infused* is that which God alone produces in the soul, without the soul contributing anything of its own except simple consent to receive God's operation and what He does within it; for this reason, it is also called *Passive* Contemplation. The *Acquired* is that which man, aided by God’s grace, acquires through his own labor, and which he exercises through his diligence and his actions; this is why it is further named *Active* Contemplation.

Man can do nothing regarding the first; it depends absolutely on God, who gives it to whom, when, and how He pleases, and who takes it away likewise without anyone being able to prevent Him—any more than all men, with all their efforts, could prevent the Sun from rising and setting.

22. (3) But all are in some way capable of the second <note>Referring to "Active" or "Acquired" contemplation, which the author suggests is accessible to all faithful people through practice.</note>; and it is a simple gaze, without <term>discourse: the process of logical reasoning or mental "conversation" used during meditation</term>, upon God or another object, which touches the will with holy affections, and particularly those of love. It is a sweet and peaceful operation of the soul...

### Part IV. Chapter VIII. § I.

24. The practice, then, of this <term>active and acquired contemplation: a state of prayer reached through one's own effort and cooperation with God, rather than a purely spontaneous mystical gift</term> consists in entering into the depths of one's spirit; and there, in the presence of God, leaving behind the senses and <term>discourse: logical, step-by-step mental reasoning or internal argument</term>, to apply oneself through faith and the <term>affections: movements of the heart and will, such as love, desire, or devotion</term> of the will toward some divine perfection, or toward some mystery of Our Lord, gazing upon Him with attention and with eyes of faith, respect, trust, and love. This is done without reasoning, and even without multiplying a vast quantity of different feelings, simply steadying oneself in this attentive and affectionate gaze. This gaze should further be simple, and so removed from all care and reflection on any other thing, that one forgets them all if possible, in order to be occupied only with looking at and listening to Our Lord—like Mary Magdalene <note>original: "la Madelaine"</note> of whom we have just spoken, and who, seated at His feet, said not a word, and though blamed by her sister...

**25. The soul must keep silence before all creatures and speak to God alone.**

The soul speaks to creatures <note>In this spiritual context, "creatures" refers to anything created—people, objects, or worldly concerns—as opposed to the Creator.</note> in four ways: In the first place, it speaks to them with the **understanding** <term>understanding: the intellect or the faculty of the mind that reasons and thinks</term>, when it thinks of them. Secondly, with the **will**, when it sets its affection upon them. Thirdly, with the **imagination**, when it pictures them to itself; and in the fourth place, with the **passions**, when it craves them—to say nothing of the language it holds with them through the external senses. So it is that the "words" the soul speaks to them are the thoughts it has of them, the affections it conceives for them, the images it forms of them, and the desires it produces for them. Conversely, the soul is silent and says not a word to them when it does not apply itself to them with these faculties, when it does not occupy itself with these operations, and when it is in a cessation of acts toward them.

28. There are certain souls who in their prayers speak constantly, being of the opinion that the secret consists in always speaking to God, and ceaselessly employing their faculties to produce "acts" <note>Formal spiritual expressions of faith, hope, or love</note>, and never listening to Him; without considering that what God will say to them will be much better and more useful for them than what they can say to Him. In the conversation and the discourse one has with another person, one does not speak to them continually; rather, one speaks, and afterwards one listens. Thus, in your prayers, speak to Our Lord, and then hear Him, making yourself attentive in silence and in respect to what He has to say to you.

#### Part IV. Chapter VIII. Section I.

29. This is how **Active Contemplation** and the **Prayer of Union** are practiced. One must note their difference from the **Prayer of Reasoning** <note>Also known as discursive meditation, where the mind thinks through religious truths</note> and the **Prayer of Affection**. In these three types of prayer, the two faculties of the soul—the **understanding** <term>Understanding: the intellect or faculty of the soul that reasons</term> and the **will** <term>Will: the faculty of the soul that loves and chooses</term>—are at work. In the **Prayer of Reasoning**, the understanding works more than the will; in the **Prayer of Affection**, the will works more. Regarding this latter form, it should be known that those beginning it do not usually enter it without some discourse <note>Discourse: sequential reasoning or internal "talking" through a topic</note>, but this gradually decreases until it ceases entirely. Furthermore, they initially have a great variety of affectionate acts <note>Formal spiritual expressions of love, desire, or devotion</note>, but in the end, far fewer. In the **Prayer of Union**, the will still predominates over the understanding, but with more simplicity than in the prayer of affection. Moreover, God works more in it, and man less; and His operation there is more spiritual, more pure, and more divine. This is why one must wait in peace and confidence for God’s action, without rushing oneself.

30. This is what led Monsieur de Renty <note>Gaston de Renty (1611–1649), a French aristocrat and mystic known for his intense piety and service to the poor</note> to say:
> "The great imperfection of souls is not waiting enough for God; and the active nature, which is not yet subdued, stirs itself, and..."

the fire was not far away and could easily spread even to them. In this common state of terror, remaining in his usual equanimity and in his abandonment to the order of God, he entered his Chapel, where he remained for a very long time in prayer <note>original: *oraison*. <margin>40.</margin> He also confessed to another confidential and trusted person that he felt himself, by the mercy of God, in a state of such complete death to all things that neither Angels, nor men, nor the loss of his loved ones, nor the ruin of his family, nor any other accident could make him lose the foundation of his peace; but that he would remain tranquil and even insensible to all of it. He said this not out of vain exaggeration or some sudden emotional impulse—which often causes one to utter things far from the truth—but through a firm and experimental <term>experimental: in 17th-century spirituality, this refers to knowledge gained through direct inner experience of God's presence</term> foundation that he possessed in the insensibility of the Saints <note>This "insensibility" is not a lack of compassion, but a supernatural detachment where one’s inner peace is not shaken by worldly disasters or personal loss.</note>.

<margin>41.</margin> Such was the mystical death and the annihilation <term>anéantissement: a central concept in 17th-century French spirituality, referring to the total emptying of one's own will to make room for God</term> of this man of God,

### Part IV. Chapter IX. § 2. ###

God, who showered him with immense treasures of spiritual riches, led him to live a most perfect life and united him intimately with Himself. For this union, that death and annihilation <term>anéantissement: a central concept in 17th-century French spirituality, meaning the soul's reduction to "nothingness" so that God can be "all" in the person</term> are absolutely necessary. This is because a being cannot become what it is not unless it ceases to be what it is. Wood cannot take on the nature of fire as long as it retains its own nature; it must leave its nature behind, and the matter must be stripped of all the "forms" of wood—both the substantial and the accidental <note>In the Scholastic philosophy of the time, the "substantial" form is the essence of a thing (what makes wood "wood"), while "accidental" forms are secondary qualities like its shape, color, or weight.</note>—and be reduced to a total nakedness <term>nudité: in mystical theology, a state of being completely stripped of all worldly attachments, sensory images, and self-will</term> so that the fire may unite with it. Without this nakedness, union is impossible.

<margin>42.</margin> It is a general rule in nature, which allows no exception, that for a subject to receive a form, it must be disposed toward it—and all the more so when the form is more noble. This disposition consists in this stripping <term>dépouillement: the active process of divesting oneself of ego and earthly desires</term> of the subject, and in the loss it must undergo of some things to gain others. Consequently, to create a divine man <note>original: *homme divin*</note>, he must no longer be a man living according to his own nature; and to make him worthy of union with God, he must necessarily die and be annihilated to himself. Certainly, if fire requires from matter this strip-

ment <note>This catchword "ment" completes the word "dépouillement" (stripping) on the following page.</note>

# The Life of Monsieur de Renty.

As this friend wished to reply and thank him, Monsieur de Renty silenced him, bidding him farewell and adding: *“this is all I had to say to you; pray for me.”*

18. A little while later, and shortly before his death, holding his eyes raised upward as if he saw something, he said: *“The Holy Infant Jesus, where is He?”* They brought him an image <note>Likely a small devotional painting or engraving of the Christ Child, a common object of prayer in the 17th-century French School of spirituality.</note> of Him, which he kissed. He asked for his crucifix; he took it and kissed it lovingly. Then, turning toward death, he entered into his final struggle <term>agony: from the Greek *agonia*, referring to the final physical and spiritual labor preceding death</term>, which lasted only a good quarter of an hour. For more than half of that time, he continually uttered the Holy Name of JESUS, and made acts of resignation and surrender <note>original: "abandon à Dieu" — a central concept in de Renty's spirituality, involving the total entrustment of one's will to God's providence</note> to God as best he could, and then expired gently. This holy soul departed, as we have great reason to believe, to his place of rest.

19. It is thus that Monsieur de Renty lived and died—one of the most brilliant lights that God placed in His Church in our century, and one of the greatest ornaments of true devotion to have appeared in a long time. He died in Paris in the thirty-seventh year of his age, in the year sixteen hundred and forty-nine, on the twenty-fourth of April around noon, at the hour of the Elevation of Our Lord upon the Cross. <note>Traditional Christian piety associates the hour of noon with the moment Jesus was raised on the cross at Calvary.</note>

->### Fourth Part, Chapter 10<-

...the Cross, of which a certain person had some knowledge that its merit <note>In Catholic theology, "merit" refers to the spiritual fruits of Christ's sacrifice on the Cross, which are believed to be applied to a person's soul to forgive sins or shorten time in Purgatory.</note> had been applied to him at the moment of his death.
