This placed him in a state to be able, at the moment of his departure, to enter into his beatitude and enjoy the presence of God.

20. Reports have been shared of revelations and visions of his glory, including that he was seen at the instant of his death as a globe of light rising from the earth to Heaven <note>The "globe of light" is a traditional hagiographic motif symbolizing the soul's purity and its direct ascent to the divine.</note>. Miraculous healings performed through his intercession are recounted, as well as help through deeds and words given to people for their spiritual advancement. None of this is incredible; on the contrary, a life as holy as his, and virtues so heroic <note>The term "heroic virtue" is a formal designation in the process of sainthood, indicating that a person practiced Christian virtues to an extraordinary degree.</note>—which made him one of the great wonders of our day—facilitate such belief and can easily persuade us of it. Nevertheless, because I do not hold these things to be as certain as those I have already described, and because the holiness and perfection of Christianity do not consist in them, and because we cannot imitate them as we can his other virtues, I shall not dwell on them further.

21. I say only in conclusion that we have great cause to admire the counsels of God <note>original: *conseils de Dieu*; referring to God’s inscrutable plans and divine wisdom</note> in this death, for having withdrawn from the world a man who did so much good there, and who could yet have done even more. Since he was in the full strength of his mind, the flower of his age, and held in a very high degree of esteem, influence <note>original: *crédit*; referring to his social standing and the trust others placed in him</note>, and capability, he could have marvelously advanced—even more than ever—the honor of God and the salvation of his neighbor.

22. But why? It is God who has done it, and that says everything. He wished to show by this, and to teach us, that He has no need of us for the advancement of His glory or the execution of His designs, and that He will succeed quite well without us. This is so that we do not think too highly of ourselves if He occasionally employs us, but that we may always be humble in His presence. Furthermore, He has called him to a place and a state where he glorifies God much more perfectly than he would have done here below; from which also it bears pre-eminently the name of the place and state of glory. This should be understood not only as the glory which the Blessed <term>the Blessed: original *Bien-heureux*; in Catholic tradition, those who have died and entered the direct presence of God in Heaven</term> receive there, but even more as the glory which they render to God. # CHAPTER XI.
## Conclusion of the Entire Work.
### *How One Ought to Read the Lives of the Saints.*

# CHAPTER XI.

## Conclusion of the entire Work.

->*How one should read the Lives of the Saints.*<-

1. To conclude this work and make its reading more useful, I believe it will be appropriate to show how one should read the lives of the Saints and the histories of excellently virtuous men, in order to gather the fruit for which they are written. St. Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD) was a foundational theologian whose *Confessions* is one of the first Western autobiographies, detailing his journey from a life of worldly pleasure to Christian faith.</note> recounts that when he was preparing for his conversion, feeling terrible pains and inexplicable anguish—particularly regarding the prospect of leaving the creatures he loved and living in continence <note>The virtue of self-restraint, specifically the choice to abstain from sexual relations.</note>—this virtue presented herself to him with a face full of majesty and sweetness. With a friendly smile, she invited him to approach, extending her charitable arms to receive and embrace him. Within those arms, he saw a great number of people whose examples could greatly strengthen him. He saw there a multitude of young people, boys and girls, men and women of all ages, wise widows, and virgins grown old in their years. And Continence, mockingly teasing him in a pleasant way intended to give him courage, said to him: *(a) Can you not do what these men and women have done? Or was it by their own power that they were able to do so, and not in the Lord their God?* <note>original Latin: *Tu non poteris quod isti & istæ? an verò isti & istæ in semetipsis possunt, ac non in Domino Deo suo?*</note> Could you not do what these boys and girls, these men and women, were able to do? As if they had done it by their own strength, and not by the help that God gave them!

19. We are therefore able to do, in our own way, what the Saints were able to do in theirs; and if we fail in this, we are guilty, and their actions

21. When we present ourselves before the Tribunal <term>Tribunal: a court of justice; here referring to the Final Judgment of God.</term> of our sovereign Judge to receive our final sentence, says St. Prosper <note>Prosper of Aquitaine (c. 390 – c. 455 AD), a prominent Christian writer and defender of St. Augustine’s teachings on grace. The work cited in the margin is now often attributed to Julianus Pomerius.</note>, what shall we do? What shall we say? To whom shall we have recourse? Shall it be to the Saints and the Friends of God, whose instructions we did not wish to receive and whose lives we did not wish to imitate? Shall we excuse ourselves based on the corruption of our nature and the fragility of our flesh? *But the examples of all the Saints will cry out against our excuses and render them useless; because, living within the fragility of the flesh without surrendering to it, but rather emerging victorious, they showed that what they did could certainly be done; especially since they did not do it, nor did they resist sin, by their own strength, but by the assistance they received from the mercy of God.* <note>original Latin: "sed excusationi reclamabunt omnium Sanctorum exempla, qui cum fragilitate carnis in carne viventes, quod fecerunt, utique fieri posse docuerunt: maxime quia nec ipsi peccato suâ virtute; sed Domini miserantis auxilio restiterunt."</note>

What then shall we answer at that time, if Our Lord says to us, as He effectively will: *If you were able, why did you not resist the desires of sin? If you were not—* <note>original Latin: "Si potuistis, quare non restististis desideriis peccatorum? si non po-"</note>

Even in the flower of his youth, born of such high rank, possessing all the advantages the world could offer, and remaining in the secular state <term>Secular state: the life of a layperson living in society, as opposed to a "religious" state like that of a monk or priest.</term>, he led a life so virtuous and so holy that he has traced for all kinds of people excellent models of virtue to imitate; or given, if they are neglected, great cause for us to receive blame.

# PREFACE.

*This work is of a very particular character: the people who wrote it have much less of a share in it than she who is its subject, or rather than the Spirit of God who inspired in her what she wrote herself. For her life is composed of little else but her own writings, and we have done nothing more than arrange them to make the work complete.*

*It is a series of very devout sentiments and celestial visions, which are well-suited to lead souls toward evangelical perfection <note>original: "perfection évangelique" — a term referring to a life led according to the counsels of the Gospel, often involving vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience.</note>, especially those who devote themselves to the exercises of the interior life <term>interior life: a spiritual practice focused on the internal relationship between the soul and God, often involving silent prayer and contemplation.</term>. They will undoubtedly find much to learn and to advance in the ways of God by observing the conduct and following the footsteps of such a great soul.*

*As the Reverend Father Saint-Jure <note>Jean-Baptiste Saint-Jure (1588–1657), a prominent Jesuit spiritual writer.</note> of the Society of Jesus, Monsieur de Renty <note>Gaston de Renty (1611–1649), a famous lay mystic and philanthropist.</note>, and Monsieur de Bernières <note>Jean de Bernières-Louvigny (1602–1659), a French mystic and treasurer of France.</note> were the primary guides of Mother of the Infant JESUS* <note>Referring to Marguerite of the Blessed Sacrament (1619–1648), the subject of this biography and a Carmelite nun renowned for her devotion to the Holy Infancy.</note>

->*Of her Vocation to the religious life.*<-

I. Our Lord, who usually grants these desires for suffering only to those Souls whom He wishes to separate from the world, inspired Mademoiselle de Baillou with the thought of withdrawing into a Monastery. [...the promise] presented the struggles she would have to sustain regarding her father and her mother, whom she loved tenderly, and by whom she was also tenderly loved. It was in this encounter that she began to experience that *love is strong as death* <note>original: "l’amour est fort comme la mort," a quotation from the Song of Solomon 8:6.</note>; since she felt within herself such terrible struggles between Grace and nature <note>In 17th-century spirituality, "Grace" refers to divine influence and the call to God, while "nature" refers to human emotions and family attachments.</note>, that she had need of arming herself with all her courage.

4. She took this first step with a firmness that surprised him: she nonetheless felt her heart as if breaking with tenderness; and she said one day to a Sister who was giving her the account of the pains she had suffered in separating from her Father, that her own had been so great, that every time she read those of Saint Teresa <note>Saint Teresa of Avila (1515–1582), a Spanish mystic whose widely-read autobiography describes the emotional agony she felt when leaving her father's house to join the Carmelites.</note>, it seemed to her that the Saint expressed what she herself had felt in that moment.

7. All these holy yearnings did not prevent her father and mother from keeping her at home. They did what they could to distract her, and even proposed a trip to **Normandy** <note>A historic province in northwestern France.</note>, with the intent of further probing the depths of her heart; and perhaps in the hope that the world, which she had not yet tasted, would make her lose the thought of **Religious life**. As she already found everything others love to be her own torment, and as she looked upon pleasures with horror, she would have liked to excuse herself from the trip: but as she was otherwise docile, and since she was not displeased to test herself, she yielded without much resistance.

8. As soon as they were in **Rouen** <note>The capital city of Normandy.</note>, they thought only of organizing parties and walks for her benefit. They added some devotion at times, to please her; and one day among others, which was **Pentecost** <note>Also known as Whitsunday, a major Christian feast commemorating the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles.</note>, they went to a chapel which is two leagues from the city. Finishing their meal, they had a strong urge to leave this place, without knowing why: but they soon recognized that **Providence** <term>Providence: The protective care of God as a power that guides human destiny.</term> was watching over them; for they had hardly taken fifty steps up the mountain when they saw the whole plain covered in water. Such a strange and surprising accident gave cause to think that the **Demon** <term>Demon: A reference to the Devil; in 17th-century hagiography, natural disasters were often attributed to the Devil's attempts to thwart the holy.</term> invented this stratagem to rid himself, if he could, of this young girl, whom he already looked upon as his enemy, and whom he foresaw would one day be so opposed to him by snatching so many souls from his hands: but **Our Lord**, who watches over the protection of those he cherishes, preserved his spouse <note>original: "son épouse"; a traditional term for a woman who has dedicated her virginity to Christ.</note> from this danger.

Moreover, she faced other causes of **mortification** <term>Mortification: The act of subduing one's desires or enduring hardships and humiliations to strengthen spiritual discipline.</term> that were quite difficult to bear at such a young age. Nevertheless, she endured everything with constancy, and did not even open her mouth to utter a single word of complaint that might have offered her comfort.

### *Concerning her entry into Religious Life <term>Religion: In this historical context, "entering religion" specifically means joining a monastic order to become a nun.</term>. But the fervor of Sister Elizabeth always prevailed over that of the others. Furthermore, although she possessed much wit, her simplicity of Grace was so great that when she had committed a fault, she would say to her companions: *“Do you see that the Holy Child JESUS is angry; it seems as if He wants to cry.”* <note>This reflects a common Baroque-era spirituality where nuns interacted with devotional statues as if they were living presences, a practice intended to foster a sense of constant companionship with the divine.</note>

## CHAPTER V.

->*How she was elected Mistress of Novices: and how she prepares herself for it by turning to God, to whom she offers her resolutions.*<-

<margin>1.</margin>The Mother Mistress <term>Maîtreſſe des Novices: the nun responsible for training and guiding the new recruits—novices—into the spiritual and practical life of the convent</term> having fallen ill at that time, eyes were turned toward Sister of the Infant Jesus, who was aged twenty-three at most, to fill such an important post. They did not listen to the reasons her humility provided to excuse herself, because she alone believed herself unworthy, while she actually possessed all the qualities necessary to exercise the role worthily: prudence, discernment, insight into the interior <note>original: "lumieres ſur l'interieur." This refers to a perceived spiritual gift for understanding the hidden state of a person's soul or their private struggles.</note>, zeal, strength, gentleness, regularity <term>régularité: the strict and consistent adherence to the Rule and daily schedule of the religious order</term>, a high regard for the matters of the Religious life <term>la Religion: here referring specifically to the monastic state and its vows</term>, and a natural gift for expressing them. This would be clearly seen in the subsequent years she spent in this role, which amounted to nearly twenty-four or twenty-five years across different periods, and where she finally ended her life.

->The Life of the Venerable Mother<-

## I. §. FIRST SECTION.

*She directs and guides souls both by her own example and by instructions, varied according to the different states of souls, leading the generous through the path of pure LOVE; the mercenary <note>In spiritual literature, "mercenary" refers to those who serve God primarily out of a desire for heavenly rewards or fear of punishment, rather than pure love.</note> through the path of rewards; others, by the path of self-discipline <note>original: "se faire violence à soi-même." A reference to the spiritual effort required to overcome one's own nature to serve God.</note> etc., and all this with enlightenment, humility, wisdom, vigilance, zeal, and charity.*

6. She began by practicing herself what she wished her novices <term>novices: individuals in a period of trial and training before taking their final religious vows</term> to practice. She was the first and the last at all activities of the Community <term>Community: the collective group of nuns living together under a shared rule</term>, exact in the smallest observances, fervent in penance, in humiliations, and in everything that can crucify nature <note>To "crucify nature" is a metaphor for suppressing physical desires and the ego to achieve spiritual growth.</note>. It seemed, by her manner of acting, that she had forgotten the great heights of her interior life to return to the basic practices of novices who are just beginning, so much did she make these practices her own, "becoming all things to all people" <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 9:22, indicating her ability to adapt her teaching to the specific needs of each soul.</note> to win them all for JESUS CHRIST.

7. She led them through a great annihilation <term>annihilation: a mystical term (French: anéantissement) referring to the total emptying of one's own will and ego to be filled by the presence of God</term>, hiding them from their own eyes. When God gave them—

[...God] granted them some special grace, or when she noticed in them some extraordinary gift of prayer <term>prayer: specifically "oraison," a form of mental or contemplative prayer as opposed to vocal prayer</term>, she would guide them back to the common and humble paths, which are nonetheless solid in virtue. She permitted them nothing unique, nothing flashy, and nothing that might attract the admiration of others <note>original: "estime des créatures." In this context, "creatures" refers to any created beings, specifically fellow humans, rather than the Creator.</note>, because she knew that such things are dangerous for young people; and since all their goodness was still only in bloom, the slightest wind would be enough to make it perish.

8. Every week, she gave them wonderful lessons on the Religious virtues: on obedience, on poverty, on precision in small matters, on the interior spirit, on silence, on the necessity of dying to everything <note>A common ascetic theme meaning to detach oneself from worldly desires and the ego.</note> in order to belong to God, and on several other important subjects. Our Sisters who had the happiness of being under her guidance have made several small collections of her discourses; however, because they perhaps did not faithfully record her thoughts, and might have diminished their strength or altered their character by adding something of their own, we will not include them here. This is because we include nothing here except what we have found written by her own hand, or else some short sayings that have remained unchanged.

9. She spared no effort to make them clearly recognize the beauty and advantages of the virtues she taught them. She presented every virtue in all the different lights that might make it loved, and always adapted herself to the spiritual inclinations of each Novice <term>Novice: a person in training to become a nun or monk who has not yet taken final vows</term>.

(1) To souls that were both noble-hearted and full of love, she spoke of the pleasure found in acting for the SOLE MOTIF OF LOVE, and showed them the value that this motive gives to all our actions.

(2) To mercenary souls <note>original: "ames mercénaires." In 17th-century spirituality, this referred to those motivated by the promise of reward or the fear of punishment, rather than pure devotion.</note>, she spoke of the *reward* that awaits the Saints, and of the Kingdom that the Heavenly Father has prepared for them since the beginning of the world.

(3) To those who were more attached to themselves, she showed the necessity of seizing Heaven by doing violence to oneself <note>A common scriptural reference to Matthew 11:12, implying that the spiritual life requires intense personal struggle and effort.</note>, by carrying one's cross, and by crucifying one's flesh in order to belong to JESUS CHRIST.

She never gave any truce to nature <note>In this context, "nature" refers to the ego, human impulses, and the fallen self which resists the work of God's grace.</note> wherever she encountered it, knowing well all its ruses and all its defenses. She went to attack it even in its stronghold, and in those places where it is most imperceptible, clearly showing that she was experienced in this kind of warfare, and that she had won great vi-

spoke in her and through her. A sister asked her a matter of importance that was difficult to resolve, because she did not want to reveal the underlying reason behind it. ## 4. §. FOURTH SECTION.

Another ten-day retreat. I. *God, the center of the soul.* II. *The life of God in us.* III. *Contemplation, or the purifying and deifying gaze of God. Its differences and properties.* IV. *Divine peace.* V. *The birth of Jesus Christ, the model of our rebirth.* VI. *His infancy.* VII. *Naked love.* <term>naked love (amour nud): a mystical term describing a pure love for God stripped of self-interest, emotional comforts, or intellectual concepts.</term> VIII. *Application to the spirit of Jesus. Belonging entirely to God,* IX. *And in His peace.* X. *Seeking the glory of God.*

### I. FIRST DAY.

46. I had a vision that **GOD** alone is the center of the soul, where it can find its true rest.

> ,, What confusion it is to see that all natural things tend with all their strength toward their center, and that my soul, through a strange disorder, does not tend there, stopping instead at so many vain and useless things that act as obstacles to its perfect happiness!

E 3

...revealed itself so clearly, that everyone noticed it, and she was forced to go to the **Infirmary**. Her fever, already quite violent, continued to increase, and lasted for more than three months. She had three violent attacks per day, which seized her with great vomiting, or by a **lethargic stupor**. This latter occurrence caused her a kind of martyrdom; for the **Physicians** having expressly recommended that she be prevented from sleeping, the affection that the sisters felt for her was the reason she was given no rest, and they tormented her at every moment to wake her up. She admitted that if God had not sustained her, she would have fallen into impatience a thousand times; but she suffered everything without complaining, except about her own <term>immortification</term><note>In a religious context, "immortification" refers to a perceived failure to discipline one's own will or body; she humbly felt her suffering was a sign of her own spiritual imperfection.</note> and the trouble she was causing others.

### 3. §. THIRD SECTION.

*Her luminous and supernatural knowledge and her sufferings in the mystical life; and her fluctuations between Heaven and Hell: in which M. de Bernières assists her through his letters.*

## § SECTION FIVE.

### *Another Six-Day Retreat of the Year 1655*

4. Nov. I. To go out of oneself to enter into God and let him enter into us. II. Sublime experiences of God, of his touches, of his sweetnesses, etc., in the depths of the soul. III. The nothingness of the soul, and the "all" of God. IV. Jesus Christ loved most that which served most for his annihilation <term>annihilation: From the French *anéantissement*, a key concept in 17th-century mysticism referring to the total emptying of the self to make room for God.</term>. Mystical sense of Psalm 43 (42) <note>In the Vulgate Bible used at the time, Psalm 43 is often the second part of Psalm 42; it begins with "Judge me, O God."</note>. V. Estimation of goods and evils. VI. Divine glory. All through Jesus Christ and in him.

## CHAPTER VII.

->How she was elected Prioress, and what her principal virtues were.<-

I. Her election was like a thunderbolt for her, and all her courage seemed to fail her in this encounter: for ultimately, however eager she was for mortifications <note>mortifications: spiritual exercises or acts of self-denial used to discipline the body and will</note> and crosses <note>crosses: a metaphor for burdens or suffering taken up in imitation of Christ’s sacrifice</note>, she could not at first resolve to receive this one, and even put everything into motion to avoid it. Seeing Heaven and earth as bronze for her <note>Heaven and earth as bronze: a biblical idiom (from Deuteronomy 28:23) suggesting that her prayers were not being answered and there was no escape from her fate</note>, since her prayers had not been able to bend the heart of

Despite her devotion to spiritual suffering, she initially recoils at the heavy responsibility of leadership.</summary>

Here, "her Spouse" refers to Jesus Christ himself.</note>, who was indifferent to her sorrow, and seeing that fellow creatures were deaf to all the reasons that her humility could suggest to make them understand her own sense of incapacity—of which she alone was convinced—she could never hold back her tears, nor stop herself from complaining, even though she had made a profession to remain mute until death in everything that might cause her distress.

2. She understood clearly, however, that the decree had been given, and that she had to sacrifice herself blindly for the public good. Thus, viewing herself at that moment as the slave of all those who were to be subject to her, she said, like JESUS CHRIST: (a) *“Behold, I come, my God, to do your will.”* <note>original: "Voici que je viens, mon Dieu, pour faire vôtre volonté." 2. Following these maxims, she wrote one day to a person of confidence in these terms:

*If you complain of your miseries, I would have incomparably more reason to form such a complaint. But after all, I believe that to advance well in the good graces of our good God, and to be among the first in His Court, one only needs to profit well from the depth of miseries with which we are so greatly enriched, and to draw from this troublesome treasure the means to pay for the mercies of God. Only a little earth is needed; nothing is needed, since only our <term>nothingness<gloss>The spiritual concept of "le néant" (nothingness), emphasizing that the human soul has no value or existence independent of God's grace.</gloss></term> is required: let us offer Him this poor nothing, and say in that spirit of humility which wins the heart of JESUS CHRIST: (a) My substance is as nothing before thee. <note>original Latin: "Substantia mea tanquam nihilum ante te."</note> [My being is like nothingness in your eyes.] Here, my God, is what I can do; here is all that I can offer you: weaknesses, infirmities, ignorance, confusion, <term>vicissitude<gloss>The tendency of the human heart to be fickle, unstable, or constantly changing in its devotion.</gloss></term>; and these are my riches: I say mine, I who speak to you.*

3. In another [letter] she says:

*Employ the ardor of your prayers for me, who leads a life quite stagnant <note>The original French "moisie" literally means "moldy" or "musty," used here to describe a soul that feels decaying or inactive due to lack of spiritual fervor.</note> in infidelity to <term>Grace<gloss>The free and unmerited favor of God, which the subject feels she has failed to respond to adequately.</gloss></term>; so much so that God must be what He is, and must grant a share of His charity to His creatures, just to suffer my presence.*

> “Those who honor us and who praise us act exactly like a person who would take another and expose them on the edge of a precipice, or on the summit of a high mountain, in evident danger of falling headlong. ### of the Child Jesus. Chapter IX.

14. Speaking of humility to a person who had confidence in her, she said to them:

> When the soul remembers its imperfections and its inclination toward evil, our good God remembers it, and grants it graces, and assists it: but when it has forgotten its misery and its corruption, the divine Lord forgets it as well, and turns His gaze away from it; for He does not love to see falsehood, but truth. Therefore, the most common exercise of the creature <note>original: "créature". In 17th-century spirituality, this term emphasizes the vast distance between a human being and God the Creator.</note> on earth must be a gentle and sincere admission of its imperfections. It is an Altar upon which we sacrifice our good opinion of ourselves, and the desire for our own excellence, to pay homage to the sovereign perfection of God: this Altar must always be prepared.

15. It also appears that her Altar was always ready, and that she often gave an account of her weaknesses, based on a response made to her by Monsieur de Bernieres <note>Jean de Bernières-Louvigny (1602–1659) was a high-ranking French official and a renowned lay mystic who provided spiritual direction to many, including the Mother mentioned here.</note>, in which he said to her:

> Go to JESUS in your spiritual weaknesses; and if you do not have the strength for it, let yourself fall at His feet, so that your weakness may touch Him, and so that there may be as many tongues within you calling for His gaze and His help as there are incapacities within you that would distance you from Him.

### CHAPTER X.

*Concerning her spirit of death and annihilation <note>In 17th-century spirituality, "annihilation" (anéantissement) refers to the voluntary emptying of one’s own will and ego to allow God to fill the soul entirely.</note>. Divine views and words on this subject, and the rules she had prescribed for herself, which she ratified through her practice.*

1. She was constantly occupied with destroying within herself that foundation of misery and corruption that we have inherited from our first birth <note>This refers to the state of "original sin" or the natural human condition prior to spiritual transformation.</note>: but one could not better understand with what passion the Mother of the Child JESUS worked toward her mystical death <note>A state where the soul is "dead" to worldly desires and its own self-interest, living only for God.</note> than through the insights and feelings that God communicated to her on this subject. An archaic French rendering of the Italian mystic's plea for rapid spiritual purification.</note>, pull me from my being, and place me into the operation of my end <note>Here, "end" means "purpose" or "ultimate goal"—the reason for which a person is created.</note> for which I am created.

And we have found written in her own hand these words, which clearly mark the desire she had to be annihilated <note>original: "anéantie"; in 17th-century French spirituality, "annihilation" refers to the total emptying of the self-will to allow God to act through the soul</note> in the minds of others, and that God might be glorified by it.

10. She often said that the truly dead <note>referring again to "mystical death," where a person is dead to their own desires and worldly reputation</note> do not speak of themselves, neither for good nor for ill; and it was one of her practices never to say anything about herself, no more than if she had never existed. She never justified herself against anything people might think of her; and in several instances which must have affected her deeply, and about which she would only have had to say a single word to make it known that she was right—and even to prove clearly that she acted by counsel <note>original: "par conseil"; meaning she was acting under the guidance of her spiritual superiors or directors rather than her own whim</note>, without stubbornness, without preoccupation, and without any interest other than the glory of God—she would not have wanted to make even a single

sign that could disabuse anyone; and remaining in the greatest peace in the world, she let people think of her whatever they wished. It was then that, defying human reason <note>original: "crevant les yeux à la raison humaine," literally "bursting the eyes of human reason," meaning she acted in a way that contradicted normal human logic or common sense</note>, she acted simply as if she had not seen what people might think; so that in whatever way her actions were interpreted, she always found that the more they were to her disadvantage, the more justice was being done to her. She acted, I say, in this manner unless charity was involved, or the honor of Divine Majesty obliged her to take another course of action.

# The Life of the Venerable Mother

The distress you feel when you are among creatures <note>In 17th-century spirituality, "creatures" refers to any created thing or person other than God.</note> shows clearly that you have found the Creator, and that all your prayer must be to remain in Him, so that He Himself may lose you in Him more and more.

When it was written to you that God had not yet come into you, this was meant in a way that requires explanation. For this purpose, my dear Sister, we shall use the comparison of a river—for example, the Seine—which flows continually to lose itself in the sea; but when it approaches, the sea, by a tide, comes as if to meet it, seemingly to urge it to hasten its disappearance; and then when it has arrived in the sea, one can say that it is truly lost, no longer existing at all: only the sea appears.

In the same way, the soul in the <term>active interior way</term> <note>original: "voie active interieure"; the stage of spiritual life where the soul actively seeks God through its own efforts, such as meditation or disciplined prayer.</note> tends toward God; it does so again in the <term>passive way</term> <note>original: "voie passive"; the stage where the soul ceases its own efforts and is moved directly by God's grace, whether through "light" (joy) or "darkness" (spiritual trial).</note> of lights or of darkness, of abundance or of poverty. The state that follows is when God Himself seeps and flows into the channel of the soul's <term>powers</term> <note>original: "puissances"; refers to the faculties of the soul—the intellect, the will, and the memory—which were believed to be the channels through which God interacts with a person.</note>, to draw them more strongly into the abyss of His infinity: and then the soul is completely annihilated <note>original: "anéantie"; a mystical term for the total surrender of the self-will, not literal destruction.</note> and lost: God alone is, lives, and operates. Now, my dear Sister, we agree that God has come into you by a secret flowing that He makes of Himself into your powers; but He will show you the mercy, if you

I am with all my heart, etc.

> When the soul is completely <term>annihilated</term> <note>original: "anéantie"; in 17th-century French spirituality, this refers to the total surrender of the self, its will, and its ego to allow God to act through the person.</note>, JESUS CHRIST exists and subsists, and the creature is no more, lives no more, and acts no more. This is the final degree of <term>consummation</term> <note>original: "consommation"; meaning the ultimate point of spiritual union where the soul is "consumed" by God’s presence.</note>, where JESUS CHRIST performs the *same mysteries that he alone performed on earth, in suffering, acting, and conversing, speaking and leading the same temporal life* that he lived on earth: and here is the wonder, that JESUS, being in Eternity, immersed in the heart of his Father, where he lives an entirely glorious life, begins to become incarnate all over again, to be born, and to live *in time*, just as he lived during his mortal life. These are the wonders of the *mystical life*; and it is the great miracle that God performs in souls who are faithful in annihilating themselves and renewing themselves in God.

### Of the Child Jesus. Chapter X, Section 3.

37. This certainly demonstrates to us the truth told to us by a great servant of God; that she possessed an admirable innocence, and that her entire life she had been a **child of grace** <note>A theological term for someone living in a state of divine favor and purity, often associated with the "spiritual childhood" mentioned in the Gospels.</note>.

This gift of innocence allowed her to see things innocently, that is to say, without dwelling on evil; so much so that she would say, *One should not find it difficult to speak to me of vices and sins; for they make, thank God, no impression on me, and nothing of them remains in my mind.*

38. Many years before her death she had reached such a great **simplicity**, that her soul no longer looked back upon all that she did, nor upon what she had to do; so that even in her <term>chapters</term> <note>The "Chapter of Faults" was a regular meeting where members of a religious community would gather to confess public breaches of the rule and receive spiritual direction.</note>, she could no longer prepare for them—although she always said very beautiful things—nor reflect on what she had said. That is to say, she let God act, abandoning herself to him for the present moment, in order to fulfill his most holy will.

39. She had such a pure intention, and aimed so directly at God in all her actions, that she never had any other motive in view but his glory. She could not even bear for anyone to suggest a human motive to her, to make her undertake something or to prevent her from it; God alone, she would say—

10. (a) May **JESUS** be your death, your life, & your everything.

We have seen with consolation the interior change which it has pleased Our Lord to give you: it is undoubtedly a special grace, for which extraordinary thanks must be rendered to him; it is a precious gift, & one that is worth more than all that your soul has received until now. Finally, it is God himself who gives himself in the depths of your soul, in truth & reality, in a manner that cannot be expressed, although you have the experience of it. It is this experience, my very dear Sister, which must now be your prayer <note>original: *oraison*; specifically referring to "mental prayer" or "contemplation," a silent form of internal communication with God.</note> & your union with God.

You well understand that this divine union is no longer formed as it was before your state was changed; for it used to be formed by means of the lights, the aids, the graces, & the gifts that your faculties <note>original: *puissances*; in 17th-century theology, this refers to the three "powers" of the soul: the intellect, memory, and will.</note> received from the goodness of God; & in this enjoyment you were united to him: & if it happened that Our Lord put you into deprivation, into darkness, into sterility <note>original: *sterilitez*; a common mystical term for "aridity," when a person feels no emotional or spiritual sweetness during prayer.</note> & into interior pains, your union then was formed through pure suffering, & in a painful state.

At present Our Lord has raised you above all these created dispositions, which, although very good & holy, make

he reduces it to nothingness. It is reserved uniquely to His omnipotence to lose souls in **mystical nothingness**, just as much as it is to draw them from **natural nothingness** through creation.

This is where **MYSTICAL THEOLOGY** <note>original: *THEOLOGIE MYSTIQUE*; this refers to an experiential, prayerful knowledge of God that transcends human reason or academic study.</note> (a) begins, which is hidden from the wise and the prudent, and revealed to the little ones. The only advice we give you, my very dear Sister, is that you interfere as little as you can with your own annihilation: since the efforts of the creature cannot reach that far, they must surrender, and God alone must work in an ineffable way.

There is only, in the depths of the interior, a secret and silent consent that God may do with His creature whatever He pleases. You will soon taste what the **rest of the center** <term>rest of the center: a state where the soul finds its "center" or focal point in God, resulting in a profound inner peace and stillness that remains even amidst outward activity.</term> is, and how one enjoys God in God Himself. You will also experience the insufficiency of all creatures, and of all created means (however holy and excellent they may be), to advance you in this blessed annihilation. This state is not possessed in its total reality all at once; but partly in reality, and partly in intellectual lights—I mean to say, that the light of it is given to the powers <note>original: *puissances*; in 17th-century spiritual writing, these refer to the "faculties" of the soul: the memory, the understanding, and the will.</note>, and then the reality communicates itself little by little. It is like the flowers that precede the fruit, which then fall; the fruit grows imperceptibly, but not all at once. The same [thing] will happen...

# CHAPTER XIII.
*Concerning the last five years of her life, assailed by several great sufferings until her death.*

<margin>1.</margin>
OUR Lord, who willed that the Mother of the Infant JESUS should walk after Him through the roughest and most painful paths, did not fail to send her all kinds of crosses and to test her sometimes by Himself, sometimes through creatures <term>creatures: (original: *créatures*) in 17th-century spirituality, this refers to any created thing or person—such as friends, enemies, or circumstances—as opposed to the Creator.</term>, as if He wished to keep the promise He had made her, saying these words to the depths of her heart, which she heard distinctly:
> *I will tear you away from the earth, and raise you up to the Cross: there you shall taste neither heaven nor earth, nothing but the bitterness of the Cross.*

# I. §. SECTION ONE.

*Her admirable constancy in suffering the removal of an eye and its consequences. Her universal detachment. She reveals her interior dispositions in a conversation with a spiritual person.*

---

<margin>15.</margin> Meanwhile, her illness, which grew worse from day to day, finally reached such an extreme that the Doctors despaired of her recovery. The membranes and nerves of the eye had become so slackened that it was completely displaced, to the point of protruding from her head the size of a small egg; it was, moreover, so black and deformed that one no longer knew what it was. The Doctors and Surgeons, greatly fearing gangrene <note>original: "la gangreine." In the 17th century, gangrene was a frequent and fatal complication of infections and was often a death sentence before the era of modern surgery and antibiotics.</note>, resolved together to remove it entirely.

The twelfth of June was the day appointed for performing such a cruel operation. The eve, which was the Feast of Saint Barnabas, she prepared herself for it anew through more fervent prayer <term>prayer (oraison): mental or internal prayer, a central practice in Carmelite spirituality involving silent conversation with God.</term> and by receiving JESUS CHRIST through Holy Communion.

<margin>16.</margin> The next day she appeared so collected throughout the morning that it seemed she was no longer of this world.

# I. SECTION ONE.

*Her admirable constancy in suffering the extraction of an eye and its consequences. Her universal detachment. She reveals her inner state in a conversation with a spiritual person.*

<margin>15.</margin> Meanwhile, her illness, which grew worse day by day, finally reached such an extreme that the physicians despaired of her cure. The membranes and nerves of the eye had become so slackened that it was completely turned outward, to the point of protruding from her head the size of a small egg; moreover, it was so black and deformed that no one knew what it was anymore. The physicians and surgeons, greatly fearing gangrene <note>original: "gangreine." In the 17th century, gangrene in the head was almost certainly fatal, as there were no antibiotics to stop the spread of infection to the brain.</note>, resolved together to extract it entirely.

The twelfth of June was the day appointed for such a cruel operation. On the eve, which was the Feast of Saint Barnabas <note>June 11th. Saint Barnabas was an early Christian apostle; his feast day was used here as a marker of time.</note>, she prepared herself once again through more fervent prayer and by receiving JESUS CHRIST through Holy Communion <term>Holy Communion: the ritual reception of the Eucharist, believed by Catholics to provide spiritual strength and union with God.</term>.

<margin>16.</margin> The next day, she appeared so recollected <term>Recollected: a state of deep, quiet spiritual concentration and inner peace, often sought by monastics before facing a great trial.</term> throughout the morning that it seemed she was no longer of this world

For the rest of her life, she was forced to submit to having her wound dressed twice a day; and if the water were even slightly too cold, or if she felt the slightest draft, it caused her new suffering. But however violent her pains were, she never showed any sign of it to the person who had wounded her <note>The "person who wounded her" likely refers to the surgeon or the infirmarian sister whose medical treatments, though necessary, caused her intense pain.</note>, and she did not even want anyone to speak to her of it.

35. She was seized by a pain in her bowels <note>original: "mal dans les entrailles"</note> so violent that it brought her nearly to her end. 36. Her inner spirit felt nothing of these bodily infirmities; and a very holy person has assured us that she had made surprising progress in perfection during the last four years of which we speak.

37. O God, what a fatal moment it is when the soul no longer belongs to God nor to itself, but to the servitude of sin and the power of darkness! A moment in which it is no longer within the friendship of God, and is thus the outcast of Heaven and earth, and the prey of hell; a moment which, being deprived of the *life of grace*, is subsequently deprived of all right to the *life of glory*, <term>Life of glory: A theological term for the eternal life of the soul in Heaven, where it sees God face to face.</term> destined for eternal punishment, worthy of tears of blood, and infinitely deplorable.

O my God! how can it be that a **rational Soul**, a Soul made for You and capable of receiving You, <note>The original French "capable de vous" refers to the theological concept of *capax Dei*, the idea that human beings are uniquely designed with the capacity to know and be filled by God.</note> could fall into the disorder of this miserable moment, or else see itself fallen into it without dying of grief?

What shall be said of those who remain not for moments, but for weeks, months, and entire years in the state of sin? Who glory in their shame, <note>original: "confusions"</note> who despise the offers of divine grace, and who—notwithstanding the agonies and tortures, the stings and remorses they endure under the imperious yoke of this cruel tyrant—delight in this hell as if in a bed of roses and violets, and neglect to seek a way out. O deplorable blindness, which prevents them from seeing that there is but a single moment that is decisive for their eternity, and that if it escapes them, they shall never have it again! through their misfortune it shall be changed into
confusion and eternal malediction. It is
there that the worm shall never die, <note>A biblical reference to Mark 9:48, depicting the unending nature of suffering in the afterlife.</note> and
that the character of the children of God, printed
indelibly upon the foreheads of these
damned Souls, will cover them with shame and re-
proach. It is there that the desire of sinners
shall perish, says the Prophet, <note>Referencing Psalm 112:10: "the desire of the wicked shall perish."</note> since there is
no longer time to think of time in eter-
nity; but rather to feel inconsolable-
ly the magnitude of one’s loss.

->THE END<-

<vocab>penance, eternal malediction, damned Souls, the Prophet, eternity, sinners</vocab>

<summary>This concluding page describes the eternal despair of the damned, who realize too late the value of the grace they discarded. It emphasizes that in eternity, the time for repentance has passed, leaving only the "indelible mark" of their baptism as a source of shame.</summary>
